title: Jeffrey Donaldson: Former DUP leader sentenced to 15 years for child sex abuse convictions
description: Statements from both victims were released after the sentencing and read out by Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers.Victim A said the impact of the crimes commi
body: Statements from both victims were released after the sentencing and read out by Det Ch Insp Leah Crothers.Victim A said the impact of the crimes committed against her did not end when the abuse ended."For years I carried shame, anger and guilt, and questioned whether I was worth protecting or worthy of being loved. "The last few years have been nothing short of a battle. "The conviction does not erase the abuse or undo the impact of what happened to me, and I will always carry the consequences of it. "But those responsible do not control me now. They forever changed me, but they will not take my future. The cycle is being broken and it ends with me."Victim B said what happened to her as a child had "affected everything since then"."What would it be like not to be afraid at night, not to wake up shaking, not to have nightmares and not to lock away every feeling I have?"What happened took away my ability to trust people and, in all honesty, I don't think I really know what trust or love truly is. Nothing can ever change what was done to me. I wish it could."I stood up, many years later, because for me this is about drawing a line in the sand and knowing that the Donaldsons can no longer hurt anyone else. "Many people get to look ahead and plan their lives with hope, I've never known what that feels like. My hope was taken away from me a long time ago."

schema.headline: Jeffrey Donaldson: Former DUP leader sentenced to 15 years for child sex abuse convictions

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
description: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.N
body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal."We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries". The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up. In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:The need for free expression of opinion in news mediaThe need for a range of views in news media across the UKThe need for a range of people controlling the media across the UKThe need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UKThe letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns. A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process."This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

schema.headline: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm

title: Hole in Neanderthal shoulder bone linked to ancient wooden spear
description: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.They say a 15mm hole fo
body: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology."The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy."It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation."The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival. But they join a small but growing body of evidence which point to the possibility that human-on-human violence was more common and goes back further than the current scientific consensus would suggest."I unfortunately see the growing body of evidence as an indication that interpersonal violence goes deep into human prehistory," Stringer told BBC News.A key piece of that evidence is a study published in 2022 of very early Neanderthal skulls from northern Spain at an archaeological site called "the Pit of Bones". It suggests that deadly violence was taking place about 430,000 years ago.Researchers found 57 healed head injuries among 20 individuals. Nine individuals had potentially fatal skull fractures. Six had similar puncture wounds at the back-left of the head. Because the wounds repeatedly occurred in almost the same place, the researchers concluded that deliberate blows were more likely than accidental damage. One skull had two wounds that had probably been inflicted with the same object.The Pit of Bones findings do not show that everyone in this population was habitually violent, but they provide strong evidence that repeated killing occurred among these people hundreds of thousands of years ago.For decades, many archaeologists linked the beginnings of organised warfare to farming, when people began living in permanent settlements and competing over land, livestock and food stores.But evidence from earlier hunter-gatherers and still older human relatives has since shown that individual killings pre-date farming by a very long way.The live scientific debate is over how common such violence was, and when sporadic attacks became organised conflict and wars between groups.The research has been published in the journal Scientific Reports.

schema.headline: Hole in Neanderthal shoulder bone linked to ancient wooden spear

title: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says
description: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.From 6 Novembe
body: Online pornography depicting strangulation or incestuous relationships will be banned from early November, the government has announced.From 6 November, it will be illegal to possess or publish porn which shows strangulation or suffocation, depicts sexual activity between people who are related or shows adults role-playing as children under 16.The new rules follow a review into porn regulation in 2025 which found depictions of choking were "rife" on popular porn sites and had helped normalise the act among young people.Conservative peer Baroness Gabby Bertin, who headed the review, said the news came "not a moment too soon".She told the Press Association the change in law would "send the unequivocal signal" to companies that host and facilitate porn, and also to wider society, that "extreme and violent content that encourages real-life harm is not acceptable".Her independent review, commissioned by former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak's government, cited an account of a 14-year-old boy asking a teacher how to choke girls during sex.It warned that people imitating such behaviour "may face devastating consequences".Non-fatal strangulation is already an offence if someone does not consent - but its depiction online is currently not illegal.Amendments to the Crime and Policing Bill, which became law in April, sought to ensure such content would be captured by the legislation and made criminal offences in England and Wales.Justice minister Alex Davies-Jones said it was not about "criminalising harmless sexual preferences".But she said "porn can shape what people think a healthy relationship looks like, especially young people". Content which "normalises, or even glorifies" violence against women can "blur the line with what is acceptable in real life", she said."If you've got this material, delete it. If you're sharing it, stop," Davies-Jones added."It's not as harmless as you may think, and after 6 November, it is criminal."The new offences each carry a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment, for publication.According to the government, this could include uploading, posting or otherwise making the content available to someone online.Possession, meanwhile, could include keeping an image stored on a phone, computer or in cloud storage, the government says.Someone found to be in possession of images depicting sexual activity involving a person pretending to be under 16 could face up to three years' imprisonment, after 6 November.Those found to be in possession of images depicting strangulation, suffocation or penetrative sexual activity between certain relatives could face up to two years' imprisonment.Porn that shows or depicts sex between step or foster-relations where one person is pretending to be under 18 will also be captured by the new offences.Durham University law professor Clare McGlynn - who has previously warned widely available extreme content normalises sexual violence - welcomed the laws taking full effect."This is a potential turning point, the commencement of these laws marking a line in the sand when we decided that we were no longer going to accept the normalisation of sexually violent content in pornography," she told the BBC.But she said questions remained over how swiftly tech platforms and regulators would act to remove and mitigate the spread of violating material."While these are criminal offences, this is not about prosecuting individuals, but transforming the online pornographic landscape and that requires the platforms and regulator to act," Prof McGlynn added.Additional reporting by Chris Vallance

schema.headline: Porn showing choking or incest to be banned from early November, government says

title: Sparks fly at the Celebrity Traitors round table and a 'terrifying' death march
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Things are hotting up a bit in the castle,
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the fifth episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Things are hotting up a bit in the castle, not least for Ross Kemp, who doesn't seem to be enjoying it very much. "I'm quite angry," he said, his brow furrowing even more than usual. "I've suffered at the hands of the traitors and now they've put heat on me, so I'm quite angry about that," he said. "They're using me like a donkey."Clearly they aren't hitching rides on him at the seaside - that would be another show entirely - he's referring to them pointing the finger of suspicion at him by making him stand out when he doesn't want to. Firstly they kept the former EastEnders star and documentary maker above ground at the grave-digging task, sparing him from being buried. In this episode, he was one of four celebrities who had to sit alone in a tomb, before one of them was murdered.This was intended to get tongues wagging about him, deflecting suspicion away from the actual traitors. Joanne McNally was convinced enough by this to say: "The vibe with Ross is off. His eyes do not close. "He has not blinked since we've been here. He is giving cyborgs."Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in UncloakedComic James Acaster, possibly the most reluctant traitor in recent memory, accurately called killing off Beckett a "chaos murder". "This is a bunch of faithful who read into everything," he said. "They go, why did this happen? And with this murder, there's no answer, and they won't suspect it's us."More accurately, he should perhaps have said: "They won't suspect me or Maya," given only two-thirds of this tactic worked.Meanwhile, the task for this episode made some of the celebrities quite jumpy. This was despite it not involving being buried alive, drinking stinky water or diving down an old toilet, all of which wouldn't have been out of place on I'm A Celebrity, Get Me Out of Here. This episode's death parade saw them having to solve puzzles to avoid being seized and held captive by guards looking like Skeletor, from He-Man and the Masters of the Universe."That is genuinely terrifying," said Pinnock as the marchers approached them on the edge of a forest. "We are literally in a horror film."Michael Sheen took each puzzle as an opportunity to flex his acting muscles, using his finest Shakespearean actor's voice to bellow out the instructions to everyone else. He should have grabbed one of the death marchers to do a quick burst of Hamlet. The celebrities were victorious though, winning all the prize money for charity, and the task ended with Kemp and James Blunt using flints to spark a flame, igniting some gunpowder to hold the death marchers at bay. At the end of the task, players captured by the death marchers were held in a cage until the round table. This included all three traitors - Hannah Fry, Maya Jama and James Acaster - as well as Ranganathan, Jerry Hall and McNallyOops, bad move. This left a traitor-free zone at the castle, where theories could fly without the traitors trying to derail them. By they time everyone was reunited at the round table, traitor shade was being thown at several celebrities. Kemp firstly had to defend himself, which he did by saying: "In my defence, I would say if I was picked to be a traitor, I wouldn't have been so paralysed on the first day about the hat [where he thought he was killed in plain sight]."And the grave thing, I don't think it would be traitorous behaviour to get everybody out before you start looking for the money, so I would say that in my defence."This seemed to work, before James Blunt was briefly questioned. But Fry - an actual traitor - came in for the most flak. YouTuber King Kenny swooped, saying: "There's no surprise that I'm going to be talking to you, Hannah. I just don't understand, how are you still here?"Because when I think about it, as a traitor, you'd be one of the first people that I would get out. But also, as the traitor, you'd be extremely good because you're very smart."He wasn't wrong, and this ignited the growing chorus of celebrities who also suspected Fry.The mathematician tried to defend heself, saying: "I've been sort of doomed from the beginning because either I was going to be killed by the traitors or, as has happened, if I don't get killed by traitors, the faithful are going to suspicious of me."When votes were cast, the vast majority were for Fry. Even her fellow traitors turned on her - both Jama and Acaster voted for her, to ensure they looked like faithfuls. "I came in here with absolutely one job and one job only on my mind, which was to catch traitors," she said before she was banished. "And I calculated every conceivable scenario except for the one that actually unfolded."This was because she was of course recruited mid-way through the series.She later added: "My fellow traitors, they had to vote for me. It was so clearly going in that direction. You know what? I didn't choose the traitor life, but oh my goodness me, that was so much fun."Back in the turret, despite comic Joe Lycett's desperate efforts to be recruited, Kenny was chosen as the next traitor, because he had been such a good faithful at the round table.  He even gleefully galloped round the castle with Miranda Hart and Sebastian "Bash" Croft after they caught Fry. That was quite an unexpected sight.

title: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: India's 'cockroach' protesters set to return despite police crackdown
description: Thousands of 'cockroach' protesters are set to return to the streets of Delhi on Friday, days after police prevented their last mass demonstration and
body: Thousands of 'cockroach' protesters are set to return to the streets of Delhi on Friday, days after police prevented their last mass demonstration and two of their leaders were jailed.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement seeking electoral reforms, has called on supporters to gather at Central Park in Connaught Place, a busy commercial district.The call follows the jailing of two CJP leaders for five days after they entered Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.What began as a campaign against alleged electoral fraud has since become a wider fight over the right to protest. Central Park is not an approved protest venue either.The Delhi High Court on Thursday declined to pass an order restraining the CJP after a local trader filed a petition citing disruptions to traffic and business as reasons why Friday's protest should not be allowed. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, meanwhile, has named the protest Lehra Do Tiranga, or Wave the Tricolour, as many Indians informally refer to the country's orange-white-green flag as Tiranga. Dipke has said he is prepared to risk arrest himself.Getting to Central Park, however, may prove difficult. Police barricades and mass detentions prevented many protesters from joining their demonstration last Saturday. Dipke has urged those unable to make it to Delhi to raise the Indian flag and protest wherever they are.The CJP has come a long way from May, when the movement began with an insult. After India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches, Dipke embraced the label and turned it into an online protest movement.By July, he and his supporters were filling the streets over examination paper leaks, in protests that forced India's education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Within months, the "cockroaches" had become one of the most visible expressions of youth anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.Now they are taking on something bigger - India's elections.At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote. The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders and deploying officers across the capital before protesters could assemble.Dipke and two senior organisers, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained from within the aircraft upon landing in Delhi. The capital was put under a sweeping security lockdown. Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses. Some struggled against the officers; others, already detained, pressed towards the bus windows, waving Indian flags.Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.The scale of the crackdown drew accusations that the authorities were determined to prevent the protest rather than police it. The CJP likened the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, telling demonstrators to go instead to Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground.But Jantar Mantar is no ordinary patch of ground. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent.The CJP accuses the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned anyway, bringing a handful of supporters. They unfurled the Indian flag and shouted slogans against Kumar. Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and violated the conditions of their earlier release.The following day, Das and Ranka were sent to Tihar Jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.With two of its key organisers behind bars, the CJP heads into Friday's protest with its leadership depleted, though Dipke insists the march will go ahead and he does not intend to back down."I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said in a video message.Police, meanwhile, are preparing for another large gathering in the heart of Delhi.Senior officers met on Thursday to discuss security arrangements and possible traffic restrictions around Connaught Place, where a demonstration could disrupt one of the capital's busiest commercial districts.The CJP's campaign is unfolding alongside a separate wave of protests by India's opposition parties, which have also accused the Election Commission of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the BJP.Last week, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other lawmakers attempted to march to the commission's headquarters in Delhi but were stopped by police and detained. Opposition politicians have since taken their grievances to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court.Among those at Monday's march was Neha Bora, a feisty leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA), who has emerged as another prominent face of the demonstrations.Detained while leading protesters last Saturday, she was later seen marching with Gandhi and his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.Although the CJP, student organisations and opposition parties have largely protested separately, their demands have increasingly converged. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP organisers and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to peaceful demonstrators.Home minister Amit Shah, meanwhile, has accused opposition parties of spreading falsehoods about the voter-verification exercise and defended the Election Commission's independence.

schema.headline: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: India's 'cockroach' protesters set to return despite police crackdown

title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
description: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.Joh
body: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.The biggest four banks collectively made around £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".What is the Budget and what could be in it?The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.The sector contributed nearly £40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.The bank levy generated £1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further £1.2bn.There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around £2bn a year.The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

schema.headline: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits

title: Is women's health content being 'shadowbanned'?
description: When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What wa
body: When Irene Breen got a notification in January 2025 that Instagram was removing adverts for her company's pregnancy pillows, she was confused. What was so offensive about a pillow?She was later told on a call with Meta that the problem was the word "pregnancy"."We had to scrub the word from our entire website… from the product name," Breen said. "We had to remove all our URLs which had pregnancy in them and rename them all."The restrictions were eventually lifted but, she said, it took 10 months of conversations with Instagram's parent company Meta - by which time her business had suffered a significant financial hit.Meta, which also owns Facebook, declined to comment on specific cases, but told the BBC that while businesses can run adverts that promote wellness, sexual health and reproductive products and services, there are restrictions to avoid users across countries and cultures having a negative experience. It's not just businesses taking out paid adverts who claim their content has been unfairly restricted.Women's health creators and charities have told us their content has been removed, had sensitivity filters added, or had its reach suppressed - a practice known as "shadowbanning".The campaign group CensHERship monitors claims that women's health content is being suppressed. In a report last month, it surveyed nearly 200 creators, clinical providers, health brands, charities, and educators - 96% of whom said they had experienced restrictions in some form.CensHERship found the number of respondents self-censoring as a result of shadowbanning had gone up, from 53% in 2025 to 65% this year. This includes using euphemistic terms such as "seggs" instead of "sex", using asterisks or emojis, and avoiding certain topics altogether.CensHERship co-founder Clio Wood said this was "really damaging", because "women's health historically has been surrounded by shame and guilt… and we are just reinforcing [that]".Are told the BBC that platforms' policies "tend to be incredibly broad, whereby more often than not, nudity is conflated with sexual activity".And this ultimately hurts audiences, Wood said."We talk to so many people who say, 'The only reason I found out about my vulval cancer was because Eve Appeal posted about those symptoms, and then I researched it and could ask my doctor the right questions'," she said.But Wood said that, since starting CensHERship in 2024, she has noticed that social media companies "can see this is something that they need to engage on now."."It's all very well the policy saying XYZ content is allowed, but if the algorithm is still flagging all of that content and suppressing it, that's where the problem comes in," she said."I think within the platforms those departments are very siloed - so what we would love is for those conversations to be much more holistic."

title: Another man admits raping woman drugged and abused by husband
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The victim looked on from the public gallery as Graham Brougham, 74, changed his plea to guiltyByJonny HumphriesRe
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The victim looked on from the public gallery as Graham Brougham, 74, changed his plea to guiltyByJonny HumphriesReporting fromat Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court and Rachael LazaroNorth WestAnother man has pleaded guilty to raping a woman who was drugged and abused by her husband without her knowledge for over 20 years.Graham Brougham, 74, is the oldest of 13 men who were charged with sexual offences against the victim after being allegedly invited into her home, in the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, to abuse her by her husband.The husband, in his sixties, has already admitted 62 offences against his wife - including rape - and has given a witness statement detailing "what he says happened".Brougham, from Northwich, was told by a judge at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court that he "should be under no illusion his sentence will be custody and a long time in custody."The victim, who held hands with a family member, watched on from the public gallery as Brougham answered "guilty" in the dock to a charge of raping her in September 2024.Image caption, Graham Brougham leaving court after admitting his guiltThe husband, who remains in custody, cannot be identified to protect the anonymity of his wife.Two other men, 59-year-old Keith Fotheringham from Dundee, Scotland; and Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport, had already admitted sexually abusing her at previous hearings.The trial of 10 other defendants accused of sexual offences against the victim has been delayed until 2 November for legal and practical reasons.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Sean Peers, 38, changed his plea to guilty and admitted sexually assaulting the woman earlier this monthThey are all alleged to have committed offences against the same victim between 2015 and November 2025.Brougham was released on conditional bail and will be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial of his co-defendants.Earlier this month, the nine women and three men of the jury, plus two female reserve jurors, were told that the husband had provided a witness statement detailing "what it is he says happened" after his guilty pleas.Judge Maurice Greene said: "That statement is a long statement and that has been disclosed to all defence counsel and it contains a lot of detail."Image caption, Alan Keelan, Jonathan Kirk and Jordan Wallace deny the charges against them and, along with seven others, will go on trial next monthThe judge said the statement contained "lots of pages and lots of documents" and that lawyers in the case were "going through it carefully", which was ongoing work.The other defendants are:Philip Wild, 58, from StockportJordan Wallace, 31, from ManchesterAlan Keelan, 42, from ManchesterJonathan Kirk, 43, from StockportRobert Stewart, 70, from StockportMohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abodeRichard Townsend, 37, from RochdaleKarl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, from SomersetDaniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable, KentDavid Graves, 59, from Ilkeston, DerbyshireThe trial continues.

title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
description: "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that
body: "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said."For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train."The bus did not overturn, it is still upright – but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved."The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added.It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured.Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform.The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France."There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene.Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord, external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers. Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel. "This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected."

schema.headline: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more
description: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he rele
body: President Gianni Infantino has apologised to the Fifa Council for his World Cup sell-off plan - but has been told he is not fit to lead unless he releases all the documents and answers key questions.The Fifa Council met in Zurich on Thursday for the first time since Infantino's secret Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal emerged.Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been given to a private investment firm.In a three-and-a-half-hour meeting, Infantino also faced questions about US striker Folarin Balogun's suspended red-card ban, the Fifa Peace Prize and funding for national associations.Hours later, Fifa released a video statement from Infantino. He had declined to speak to or take questions from the media, including the BBC.In the Fifa video, he said: "First of all I apologised for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise project which led to many consequences."But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal and in no way a done deal, that actually intended to enable Fifa to invest more in our member associations, as opposed to replacing support from existing resources."Infantino said he would answer questions in writing "in due course" following what he said had been a "constructive discussion" with "different opinions and points of view".Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt - a Fifa vice-president - said afterwards that many questions remained unanswered despite the "most robust, most frank, most open Council meeting" she had experienced."One of the disappointing things is that we didn't get answers to anything that we had specifically requested - for example getting the papers from FFE," Hewitt said."I asked the question 'why not?' - and we were asked to submit those questions in writing."I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn't answer those questions now, he's not fit to be Fifa president - and that was what was shared in the meeting."Hewitt added: "I've repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven't received them and still in spite of the request today, I haven't received them."It is the rationale for why FFE happened in the way that it did, the Balogun case, the Peace Prize."The responses to those questions, which I still don't have answers to, will determine from my personal point of view whether or not Gianni is the right candidate."That will be the point at which or not we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted because until we see what actually happened it's very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change."Hewitt acknowledged there had been "some contrition" in Infantino's apology."Then there were no holds barred in terms of what we felt about what had happened," she added."What he really apologised for was not bringing it to the Council. If you regret it that deeply, share it with us."Uefa - European football's governing body - has been one of Infantino's fiercest critics and has repeatedly called on him to stand down.It has prepared criminal legal proceedings against Infantino and lodged a claim in three US courts for all documents related to FFE to be released. Hewitt hopes Infantino now freely releases the documents so the Council can understand what happened.  "Those papers coming to Council are a crucial next part of us feeling comfortable as to what, if any, criminal proceedings need to take place," Hewitt said.Asked if there was any change in stance from Uefa about Infantino, she added: "From my position, nothing has shifted. I've no new information that makes me feel any differently, other than we do have a president who is apologetic."Infantino will stand for re-election as Fifa president for a third time in March, and as yet no credible candidate has emerged to challenge the Swiss-Italian.Former Tottenham and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega has said he intends to run, but it appears unlikely he will get the five letters of support from member associations let alone be a serious contender.Senior figures within European football have told BBC Sport they want former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger to run.But it is unclear whether Wenger would be prepared to give up his position as Fifa's global head of football development for a fight against his boss that he may not win.Hewitt accepted Uefa - and Infantino's other opponents around the world - must find someone to put their name on the ballot before the deadline of 18 November.She also indicated it would be important for the president to have a rival after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023."I think it's important to Gianni to have somebody who stands with a different manifesto, and good for Fifa to have that choice," Hewitt added."We're in a democracy here. We must remember there are 211 associations and it's really important that all 211 associations have the opportunity to vote according to how they feel."This is somebody first and foremost who puts football first right at the heart of everything that they do. Secondly, it has to be somebody who unites the world. Thirdly, somebody who needs to have the courage to bring about reforms."Hewitt said Balogun avoiding a suspension after being sent off at the World Cup was one of the "biggest issues".Balogun's ban was suspended after US President Donald Trump asked for the decision to be reviewed.BBC Sport understands a proposal was put to the Council to amend the Fifa disciplinary code, which would prevent a repeat. Under that, regulations would be amended to state the disciplinary committee could not suspend an automatic one-match ban for a red card.Fifa's legal committee will review and update Fifa Council in December."What happened in July did not serve football... whether it's the Balogun case, the FFE case... the reputation of football was put under serious threat," said Hewitt."Once behaviour starts to influence what happens on the pitch, then I think it's a dark day for football and a number of people said that in the room."The Fifa Peace Prize - awarded to President Trump - was also raised, but Hewitt said Infantino's behaviour with "other maybe celebrities and dignitaries" was also discussed."When he puts other dignitaries in front of his 211 associations, then he's lost what football is about," Hewitt said."And that was said by a number of people, not just the Europeans."How the Peace Prize came to be awarded will be the subject of an investigation by the Fifa social committee which will report back in December. "They will consider, first of all, how the Peace Prize came about, whether it should have come about, whether it should have been awarded in the way that it was, who made that decision and whether or not it should be taken out or whether it should be reformed," Hewitt said."That committee will report back to Council in December and then Council will make the decision based on its recommendation."Today there was a watershed moment where it's very clear in order to move forward, which we all want to do, we have to understand the past."

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa president apologises over World Cup move but told he must do more

title: Mother of Henry Nowak killer could be deported
description: The mother of murderer Vickrum Digwa could be in line for deportation from the UK, the Home Office has signalled.Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three
body: The mother of murderer Vickrum Digwa could be in line for deportation from the UK, the Home Office has signalled.Kiran Kaur, 53, was jailed for three years in July for removing the knife used by her son, Vickrum Digwa, to kill student Henry Nowak from the crime scene.However Kaur, who spent several months on remand, could serve less than half of her sentence and be freed around the anniversary of Mr Nowak's death under the Government's early release scheme, ITV News reported., externalThe Home Office and Ministry of Justice declined to comment on individual cases, but said: "We will always seek to deport foreign criminals at the first opportunity."Kaur, who is an Indian national, could be eligible for the government's deportation scheme.She is also appealing against her sentence, with a hearing scheduled at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.Kaur's son Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years on 1 June for the murder of the 18-year-old student, after falsely claiming Mr Nowak had racially abused him in Southampton on 3 December.Some 5,000 prisoners are scheduled to be released in stages over the next year, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and the most serious child sex offenders.Ministers say the expanded early release scheme is needed to prevent the justice system from collapsing, after a summer when the issue dominated news headlines.Some 650 criminals were this week released from prisons around the country under the scheme, less than two weeks after 700 were set free early.The Home Office said: "Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Henry Nowak, whose life was cruelly cut short in a horrific act of violence."

schema.headline: Mother of Henry Nowak killer could be deported

title: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children
description: "The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount.  It saved her life," said Stacey."It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely g
body: "The fact that they had a test there available to her was paramount.  It saved her life," said Stacey."It's a miracle she's here and we're extremely grateful for that," added Willow's dad, Russ.With the right treatment, Willow was eventually able to recover from her infection, but needed several months in hospital. She is one of many patients at the children's hospital to benefit from the new type of testing.During a study in 2024-5 metagenomic testing was used on 122 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU) at GOSH.The results have now been published in the Lancet Microbe.Metagenomic testing analyses all genetic material in a sample and can detect thousands of different pathogens. By contrast, the most common method of identifying bacteria is by trying to culture them in Petri dishes, a technology that has been used since Victorian times.Another test, PCR, can identify viruses and some bacteria, but doctors need to specify what they are trying to detect.Metagenomics testing at GOSH was able to identify around nine in 10 bacteria and viruses and all fungi in samples.In a quarter of cases, the results influenced prescribing decisions, including starting, stopping or changing an antibiotic.Dr Sam Ray, consultant in paediatric intensive care medicine at GOSH and co-author of the study said traditional testing required clinicians to make an educated guess about which infection they were looking for. "The study has helped us to spot infections we would have missed, get children on the right treatment and stop antibiotics when we know they aren't going to work."Removing unnecessary treatment is incredibly important for the fight against growing antimicrobial resistance."Metagenomic testing at GOSH also detected 50 organisms not identified by routine diagnostics, meaning it could play an early warning role against new infections.Dr Julianne Brown, head of the GOSH Metagenomics Service and co-senior author of the study said the new testing was being gradually rolled out to around 30 intensive care units across the UK treating both adults and children."It could be a powerful tool for identifying new infections that pose a pandemic threat," she added."In the future, if there was to be a new mystery pathogen that could be a cause of the next pandemic, we would detect that very quickly and put the right measures in place."The project at GOSH builds on trials at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Trust which first used metagenomics to test for respiratory infections in adult patients.

schema.headline: Same-day test helps doctors detect hidden infections in critically ill children

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
description: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previo
body: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die"."I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said.After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.  The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said. John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise"."It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said.He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan. "The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system."He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision.Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.

schema.headline: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
